title-group.article-title: Timing of Pedestrian Radiant Heat Exposure for Urban Shade Planning: A Time-Series Classification of Mean Radiant Temperature in Florence, Italy

abstract.p: Daily summaries of mean radiant temperature (MRT) give little indication of when shade is most needed on a street. This study examines whether locations with similar daily MRT ranges experience peak radiant exposure at different hours and how that distinction can inform shade planning. Hourly MRT was simulated with Lean Urban Comfort Intelligent Digital Twin (LUCIDiT) on a 1 m grid for a 2.8 km2 district of Florence, Italy, over four August days of a typical meteorological year (TMY). K-means grouped the 96-hour pixel histories into four classes. Each class was characterised by its area share, mean daily MRT range and Thermal Asymmetry Index, the difference in mean MRT between later and earlier windows of the simulation day. The morning and afternoon exposure classes together covered 40.0% of the outdoor area. Their mean daily ranges were similar (51.0 and 52.6 °C, respectively), but their asymmetry indices differed by 19.0 °C (−10.3 and +8.7 °C). Open spaces accounted for 38.4% of the area and predominantly shaded locations for 21.6%. The hourly profiles distinguish exposure patterns that are difficult to discern from the class-average daily ranges. Mapped at street scale, these patterns can help planners identify where observations of pedestrian use would inform the siting of shade.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Climate change is increasing both the frequency and the intensity of urban heat, and the urban heat island adds to this regional warming at the scale of streets and squares [1], [2]. For people walking or waiting outdoors, heat stress depends less on air temperature than on the radiant load they receive. This load is summarised by the mean radiant temperature (MRT), which combines the shortwave and longwave radiation exchanged between the human body and the surrounding surfaces, sky and vegetation [3], [4], [5]. On clear summer days MRT can differ by more than 30 °C between a sunlit square and a shaded pavement a few metres away, while air temperature differs by only one or two degrees [6], [7]. The difference matters for health as well as comfort: in Stockholm, models based on MRT explained heat-related mortality better than models based on air temperature [8].

Shade is the most direct way to reduce this load. Field measurements in Central European street canyons have shown that the reduction of MRT under building and tree shade depends strongly on the radiant fluxes reaching a pedestrian from the side, not only from above [9], and that the effect depends on street orientation, aspect ratio and tree canopy [10]. In hot, dry Tempe, shade from buildings reduced daytime MRT more than tree shade or lightweight structures, while all shade types retained some heat after sunset [11], and shade lowered the thermal sensation reported by pedestrians in every season except winter [12]. Model studies have reached a similar conclusion for canyons of different orientation [13] and have shown that the cooling obtained per street tree depends on which side of the street the tree shades [14]. A common thread runs through these studies. Whether a given piece of shade is useful depends on where the sun is when people are present.

Producing MRT maps that can capture these differences across a city district is computationally demanding. Fully coupled microclimate models, such as ENVI-met or general-purpose computational fluid dynamics (CFD) codes, resolve airflow, heat transfer and radiation together but are usually limited to small domains and short periods [15], [16]. Coupled workflows that link microclimate, building-energy and radiation tools add flexibility but not speed [17], [18], [19]. Radiation-oriented models such as Solar and LongWave Environmental Irradiance Geometry (SOLWEIG) reduce the cost by computing shadows and view factors from digital surface models [20], [21], [22], and data-driven surrogates trained on simulation output can produce MRT maps in near real time [23], [24]. Even so, continuous multi-day simulations at metre resolution over entire districts remain expensive with most of these tools. The Lean Urban Comfort Intelligent Digital Twin (LUCIDiT) model used in this study was developed to remove this bottleneck. It separates the geometric and radiative computations, approximates material thermal inertia with a recursive filter, and can generate hourly MRT maps for several days over areas of a few square kilometres [25].

A four-day run produces 96 hourly maps of the same district. Following the exposure history of a particular pavement across that many maps is cumbersome. The usual response is to summarise each location by a daily statistic, such as the mean, the maximum or the range. Heat-vulnerability indices prepared for city-wide risk management follow the same logic: they combine indicators of exposure with social and demographic layers and map one value per area [26]. A daily value is easier to read, but it can assign the same number to opposite pavements of one street even when one receives direct sun early in the day and the other late. Research on personal heat exposure has shown that the heat a person actually experiences depends on where that person is at each hour, and that exposure is misclassified when individuals are assigned fixed, area-averaged conditions [27]. Epidemiological work points the same way: in several U.S. cities, heat-related mortality was more closely coupled to afternoon and maximum temperatures than to other times of day [28]. For shade planning, the timing of exposure is part of the hazard, not a detail that can be averaged away.

Machine learning (ML) has been applied widely in urban microclimate research, but mostly in a predictive, supervised form. Regression models and neural networks are trained to map geometric and land-cover descriptors onto MRT, the Physiologically Equivalent Temperature or air temperature, so that new configurations can be evaluated without running a physical model [24], [29], [30], [31], [32]. Classification, in contrast, has mostly been driven by morphology. The Local Climate Zone (LCZ) scheme groups urban areas by built form and land cover [33] and has been used to compare outdoor thermal comfort across zones, for instance through ENVI-met simulations in Nagpur [34] and field campaigns in Lisbon [35]. Satellite studies have clustered land surface temperature (LST) to describe surface heating patterns [36], [37], [38], [39]. LST, however, describes two-dimensional surface temperature at coarse resolution and only at overpass times, and it cannot be translated directly into the three-dimensional radiant environment of a pedestrian.

Unsupervised clustering of time series offers an alternative. Instead of starting from morphology and predicting temperature, it starts from the thermal response itself and groups locations that behave alike over time [40], [41]. The approach has been used to classify LST time series in Wuhan with Euclidean, dynamic-time-warping and shape-based distances [42], to build a global taxonomy of diurnal and seasonal surface heat island cycles with K-means [43], and to group 107 Cambridge courtyards by their simulated diurnal thermal comfort with self-organising maps [44]. These studies worked either with satellite surface temperature or with a limited set of sites. Time-series classification has not yet been applied to continuous, metre-scale MRT covering a whole urban district, where it could show at what time of day, as well as where, pedestrians receive the highest radiant load.

We examine whether streets with similar daily MRT ranges reach peak radiant exposure at different hours in a 2.8 km2 district of Florence, Italy. Hourly MRT histories simulated with LUCIDiT were grouped into four classes. We compared their mean daily ranges and earlier and later exposure windows, then examined how the classes were distributed across streets, squares and green spaces. The planning question is where this temporal distinction would make a difference to site screening and what information on pedestrian use would be needed before a design could be chosen.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes the study area, the simulation and the classification. Section 3 presents the class indicators, the hourly profiles and the spatial pattern. Section 4 discusses the meaning of the timing contrast, the methodological choices, the relation to earlier work and the implications for shade planning, and sets out the limitations. Section 5 concludes.

It was selected because it combines several urban forms within a short distance: narrow street canyons, open squares, dense residential blocks from different periods, and green areas ranging from lawns to tree-lined avenues. Streets run in several directions, so that the district contains canyons whose two sides receive direct sun at different times of day.

caption.title: Study area in Florence and its 1 m digital model

sec.p: Florence lies in a transition zone between the humid subtropical (Cfa) and hot-summer Mediterranean (Csa) climates of the Köppen–Geiger classification [45], [46]. Winters are mild and humid; summers are hot and often sultry, with recurrent heatwaves and convective storms. According to the 1991–2020 climatology of the LaMMA Consortium [47], the annual mean air temperature is 15.5 °C and the summer mean 24.5 °C, with recorded extremes of −10.2 °C and 41.3 °C. Mean relative humidity is about 70%, ranging from about 80% in winter to about 65% in July. Within the district, a pedestrian can move between direct sun and canopy or building shade over a few metres, and the simulations used here resolve the resulting differences in radiant exposure.

sec.title: 2.3. Classification of hourly mean radiant temperature histories
sec.p: Each outdoor pixel was represented by a vector of 96 hourly MRT values, and the full set of vectors formed the data matrix to be classified. K-means was chosen because it is simple, scales to millions of observations and returns class centroids that can be read directly as mean hourly profiles [53], [54], [55]. It partitions the data into $k$ groups by minimising the within-class sum of squared Euclidean distances:

Distances were computed hour by hour in degrees Celsius, so that each profile kept its original amplitude and its position on the simulation clock. Two consequences of this choice should be stated. First, a pixel that is sunlit in the morning and one that is sunlit in the afternoon are far apart even if their daily ranges are similar, which is the distinction this study set out to examine. Second, because the series were not rescaled, hours in which MRT differs strongly between pixels contribute more to the distance than hours in which it differs little. In practice the classification is driven mainly by daytime conditions, when direct sunlight separates sunlit from shaded locations, and much less by the night, when MRT varies over a narrower range across the district.

The four days were concatenated in chronological order. Each hourly value therefore contributed to the distance calculation, and differences between days remained in the series. Each pixel was assigned to the nearest centroid over the full 96 hours. The algorithm used K-means++ initialisation [56] and ten random starts, retaining the solution with the smallest within-class sum of squares.

The number of classes was fixed at four. In a mid-latitude summer, a pedestrian location can be sunlit for most of the day, shaded for most of the day, or exposed mainly in the earlier or mainly in the later part of the day, depending on the orientation of the street and on nearby obstructions [11], [13]. These four conditions correspond to different shade responses, and the study asked whether a district map could distinguish them. The choice sets the resolution of the comparison; the analysis does not estimate an optimal number of classes, and the consequences of this choice are discussed in Section 4.2.

sec.title: 2.4. Class descriptors
sec.p: Each class was described by three quantities: its share of the outdoor area, the mean daily MRT range of its pixels and their mean Thermal Asymmetry Index. The Thermal Asymmetry Index compares mean MRT over two windows of the simulation day, 09:00–12:00 (AM) and 14:00–17:00 (PM):

Positive values indicate a location that is warmer in the later window, and negative values one that is warmer in the earlier window. The daily range is the difference between the maximum and minimum hourly MRT of a day:

Both indicators were calculated for each pixel and day, averaged across the four days and then summarised by class. The 24-hour range includes nocturnal cooling. The two windows have equal duration and fall on either side of midday on the simulation clock. The same simulation clock was used for all reported hours.

The classes were then interpreted in two steps. Their mean hourly profiles were examined to identify when each class reaches its highest MRT and how it behaves at night. The class map was then compared visually with the street pattern, the location of squares and the distribution of tree canopy shown in Figure 1. Because the same geometry was used to drive the radiative model, this comparison helps to interpret the classes but cannot validate them independently.

sec.title: 3.1. Class shares and daily indicators
sec.p: Table 1 gives the area and the daily indicators of the four exposure classes. Open spaces formed the largest class (38.4% of the outdoor area). The two directional classes were almost equal in size, with 20.4% for afternoon exposure and 19.6% for morning exposure, and together covered 40.0% of the outdoor area. Predominantly shaded locations accounted for the remaining 21.6%.

caption.title: Outdoor area and mean daily MRT indicators by exposure class

sec.p: Open spaces and afternoon-exposed locations had the same mean daily range (52.6 °C), yet their mean asymmetry differed by 8.7 °C. The morning exposure class had a comparable range (51.0 °C) but a negative asymmetry (−10.3 °C). The two directional classes thus differed by 19.0 °C in asymmetry, while their ranges differed by only 1.6 °C. Measured by range alone, three of the four classes, covering 78.4% of the outdoor area, fell within 1.6 °C of one another. Only the predominantly shaded class stood apart, with a mean range of 40.2 °C, about 11–12 °C below the other three, and a small positive asymmetry (+1.9 °C).

The labels morning exposure and afternoon exposure identify the earlier- and later-peaking class profiles, respectively. They describe the timing of the modelled radiant load at pedestrian locations, not the orientation of a surface. Street orientation can help explain the contrast: on a north–south street, the pavement along the west side lies in front of east-facing façades and receives direct sun in the first part of the day, while the pavement on the east side receives it later.

sec.title: 3.2. Hourly mean radiant temperature profiles
sec.p: Figure 2 shows the class-mean hourly profiles over the four days. The earlier peak of class 2 and the later peak of class 1 recurred on all four days. The morning exposure profile rose earliest after sunrise and reached values close to its daily maximum, slightly above 50 °C, several hours before the other classes peaked; it then remained high for a few hours and declined while the open and afternoon profiles were still rising. The afternoon exposure profile rose more slowly and reached its maximum, about 55–56 °C, several hours after the morning class had reached its plateau and close to the time of the open-space maximum. The open-space profile combined the early rise of the morning class with the late maximum of the afternoon class, which is why its asymmetry index was close to zero.

The predominantly shaded class had a flatter daytime profile, with class-mean maxima of about 42–44 °C, roughly 12 °C below the open and afternoon classes. At night the order of the classes reversed. The shaded profile remained the warmest, at values several degrees above the open-space profile, while the open-space profile fell to single-digit MRT values before sunrise. At night, shortwave heating ceases and the modelled radiant balance depends on longwave exchange with the sky and surrounding surfaces, whose temperatures reflect the model’s heat-storage approximation [25]. Locations with a small view of the sky exchange more longwave radiation with warm walls and canopies and less with the cold sky, so their MRT stays higher. These low night-time values in open spaces contribute to the large 24-hour range of that class. No night-time MRT measurements from the district were available to check their magnitude.

All four mean profiles fell sharply late in the simulation day. Peak timing varied less from one day to the next than peak magnitude (Figure 2). The recurrence of the early and late peaks is consistent with the influence of the fixed street geometry over this four-day period.

sec.title: 3.3. Spatial distribution
sec.p: The spatial pattern of the classes was consistent with the street layout (Figure 3). Open spaces covered the squares, the large intersections and the wider avenues, including the broad avenues that cross the district. Predominantly shaded areas occurred along tree-lined streets, in the parks with dense canopy in the western part of the district and in narrow internal courtyards. In the parks, shaded pixels formed a speckled pattern that followed individual tree crowns, with open-space pixels in the gaps between them.

caption.title: Spatial distribution of the four exposure classes

sec.p: The two directional classes often formed narrow bands on opposite sides of a street. Along many streets a band of morning exposure ran along one kerb and a band of afternoon exposure along the other, with open-space pixels in the middle of wider carriageways. The width of these bands varied with street width and building height. In narrow streets the directional bands occupied most of the cross-section, whereas in wide streets they were confined to strips close to the façades. Because the same urban geometry supplied the radiative model, this correspondence is qualitative and cannot independently validate the classification.

sec.title: 4.1. Daily range and the timing of exposure
sec.p: The mean daily MRT range was identical for the open and afternoon classes and only 1.6 °C lower for the morning class. Together these three classes covered 78.4% of the outdoor area. Their hourly profiles nevertheless differed: the open-space profile remained high across both windows, whereas the two directional profiles peaked at different hours. These class averages show what a range statistic leaves unspecified. For an individual pavement, the relevant question is whether the period of high radiant load coincides with the use that a proposed shade structure would serve.

The timing of exposure can matter beyond the difference in MRT itself. Studies of heat-related mortality have reported associations with afternoon and maximum temperatures [28] and have examined the role of radiant exposure [8]. In Florence, the simulations identify where radiant loads peaked relatively late. Establishing whether those pavements merit priority requires local information on pedestrian numbers, waiting times and concurrent weather. A market or school entrance used chiefly in the morning could warrant the opposite timing of shade.

The order of the class means reversed at night. The predominantly shaded class had lower daytime peaks and higher night-time MRT than the open-space class, a pattern consistent with field observations of some shaded settings [11]. For a square used after sunset, the difference makes evening observations particularly relevant. The present simulations quantify radiant conditions; assessing evening comfort would also require wind, air temperature and humidity at pedestrian height.

sec.title: 4.2. Methodological considerations
sec.p: Euclidean distance compares MRT values at corresponding hours on the simulation clock. A large temperature difference between two pixels carries more weight in the squared distance than a small one, irrespective of the hour. Standardising each hour separately would change that weighting and could give greater influence to hours with little spatial variation. Shape-based or time-warping approaches instead allow shifts or local changes in timing [40], [41]. Such alignment can be useful when the clock hour is incidental [42]. Here the early and late peaks in Figure 2 are precisely the distinction of interest.

K-means favours compact classes of similar spread and assigns every pixel to exactly one class, even when its history lies between two class profiles [54], [55]. Pixels at the edge of a shadow or beneath a sparse tree crown may have intermediate histories and are assigned to whichever centroid is nearest. The class boundaries in Figure 3 are better read as zones of gradual transition rather than sharp lines. A soft or probabilistic method would return, for each pixel, a degree of membership in each class, which could be useful for identifying such transition zones.

The four-class partition corresponds to the planning distinction between open, predominantly shaded, early-exposed and late-exposed locations. A finer partition could distinguish sites with brief exposure from those with prolonged exposure within either window. The present analysis does not establish how many classes the data support or how the mapped boundaries would change under independent initialisations.

sec.title: 4.3. Comparison with previous studies
sec.p: The four regimes identified here agree with what is known from street-canyon studies. Numerical work on canyons of different aspect ratio and orientation has shown that the timing and duration of direct sun on the pavements of north–south and east–west streets differ systematically [13], and measurements in Freiburg showed that the effect of street design on MRT depends on orientation and on the presence of tree canopy [9], [10]. Field measurements in Tempe found that shade from buildings and trees reduces MRT by much more than it reduces air temperature, with differences depending on orientation and shade type [7], [11]. The present results show that these patterns can be recovered from simulated MRT histories without any prior geometric rule, and that they occupy a large share of a real district.

Table 2 places the approach alongside other ways of classifying or mapping urban heat. LCZs classify neighbourhoods of several hectares by their built form and are well suited to comparing districts or cities [33], [34]. Satellite-based studies cluster LST at the scale of tens to hundreds of metres and capture seasonal and diurnal surface patterns [37], [39], [42], [43], but surface temperature is not the radiant load received by a pedestrian. The courtyard study of Peng et al. [44] is closest in spirit, since it grouped sites by their simulated diurnal comfort, but it dealt with a set of enclosed spaces rather than with a continuous street network. Supervised ML surrogates of MRT [24], [29] aim to predict MRT values for new configurations, whereas the classification proposed here summarises existing values in a form that supports decisions. The same LCZ can contain all four exposure classes, so the two schemes answer different questions and can be used together.

sec.title: 4.4. Implications for shade planning
sec.p: Shade at an unoccupied site offers little immediate relief to pedestrians. The class map does not by itself tell planners where to act, but it narrows the search and indicates which information is needed next. Figure 4 outlines a screening procedure that starts from the class map and leads to the testing of specific designs. The first four steps correspond to what was done in this study; the remaining steps describe how the map could be used in practice and were not carried out here.

caption.title: Workflow from exposure classes to shade planning (solid boxes: this study; dashed boxes: proposed follow-up)

sec.p: The key step is the overlay of the class map with information on use. Pedestrian counts, the location of seating and waiting areas, school timetables and transit schedules indicate who is present in a space and when. Matching the exposure window of each class with the hours of use then identifies sites where radiant load and presence coincide. This step requires the simulation clock and the local clock to be aligned. Table 3 summarises how each class might be treated in this screening.

sec.p: In an open square, observations of where people sit or wait can narrow the choice of sites for a canopy or tree. Heritage restrictions and underground services may favour removable shade. On a street with two directional classes, a count on each pavement during occupied hours can establish whether the busier side also receives the greater radiant load. The answer could differ for a shopping street and a school approach, even if their profiles have similar shapes. Street orientation affects the radiative benefit of tree placement [14], and whole-trip measures can extend a site assessment to the routes that pass through it [57].

The predominantly shaded class has a different role. Mapped stretches of predominantly shaded ground can be compared with walking routes to locate breaks in shade. Where those stretches coincide with tree cover, a site visit could establish which trees shade the accessible path during occupied hours. The idea links to the climate shelters that some cities designate for heat episodes. In Barcelona, the city has designated more than 200 public spaces as climate shelters, and research there has shown that access to them, and the needs of the most vulnerable residents, are uneven [58]. A map of exposure timing could help to connect such shelters with shaded routes that are usable at the hours when residents need them.

Two cautions apply. First, the classes describe radiant exposure, not thermal comfort. Comfort indices such as the Physiologically Equivalent Temperature or the Universal Thermal Climate Index also depend on air temperature, humidity and wind [59], [60], and the ranking of sites could change once these are included. Second, the candidate measures in Table 3 are options, not tested solutions. Their effect should be estimated by simulating the proposed geometry and comparing hourly MRT along the affected routes and at the occupied locations, as shown in steps 7 and 8 of Figure 4.

sec.title: 4.5. Limitations and future research
sec.p: These results describe a single district during four days of a typical summer. Other seasons, cloud conditions and latitudes change the duration and timing of direct sun, and the class shares reported here should not be transferred to other periods without new simulations. Because the weather input was a TMY, the analysis describes typical hot conditions rather than an extreme heatwave, during which the contrast between classes may be larger.

The classes derive from simulated MRT. LUCIDiT has been compared with measurements elsewhere [25], but no measurements from this district were used. Uncertainty in the modelled night-time MRT, which depends on the heat-storage approximation, affects the reported daily ranges more than the asymmetry index, which is computed from daytime windows. Measurements of MRT at a small number of contrasting sites, for instance on the two pavements of a north–south street, in an open square and beneath dense canopy, would provide an external check on both the profiles and the class assignment.

Four classes were specified for planning purposes. Neither the sensitivity of the class boundaries to the number of classes nor their stability across random initialisations was established, and the modest separation expected in continuous spatial data calls for caution at class boundaries. A class-wise comparison with sky, wall and vegetation view factors would quantify the relationship between the classes and the model geometry. Finally, the screening procedure in Figure 4 has not yet been applied with real data on pedestrian use. Future work should test the classification across seasons, numbers of classes and initialisations, compare it with measurements, and apply the full screening procedure to a set of candidate sites, using paired simulations of existing and proposed shade layouts to estimate the change in hourly MRT along specific routes.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: In this Florence district, the morning and afternoon exposure classes occupied 40.0% of the outdoor area. Their mean daily MRT ranges differed by 1.6 °C, whereas their later-minus-earlier MRT contrasts differed by 19.0 °C and had opposite signs. A third class, open spaces, had the same mean daily range as the afternoon class but virtually no contrast between the two windows. The timing of radiant exposure therefore distinguishes street environments that look similar when compared by their class-average daily range.

The classes formed a pattern that can be read in terms of the urban fabric. Open spaces covered squares and wide streets, the two directional classes formed bands on opposite sides of streets, and the shaded class followed tree-lined streets, dense canopy and narrow courtyards. The predominantly shaded class had the lowest daytime peak and the highest night-time MRT in the class-mean profiles.

For municipal shade planning, the map offers a way to screen sites before designs are compared. It indicates where radiant exposure is concentrated in the earlier or later part of the day, and it identifies the information on pedestrian use that is needed to decide where shade would be used. The decision at a particular stop, pavement or square still depends on its hours of use, the position of existing shade and the space available for trees or structures, and the effect of any proposed intervention requires a separate design simulation. Tests across seasons, numbers of classes and random initialisations, together with measurements at contrasting sites, would show how reliably the mapped boundaries recur.
